title: Debris Disposal Meeting at Lahaina Civic Center: December 18, 2023

recap.headline: Lahaina wildfire debris removal plan and search for a permanent ash disposal site
recap.in_60_seconds: County of Maui, FEMA and U.S. Army Corps of Engineers officials held a community meeting at Lahaina Civic Center on the next phase of the wildfire cleanup, which is removing debris and ash from Lahaina. The Army Corps said debris removal in Lahaina should begin in mid-January, with ash going first to a temporary storage site being built at the Olowalu cinder pits. The County said no permanent disposal site has been chosen; it scored eight sites, and Olowalu ranked first on infrastructure and health criteria. Officials answered about 25 written questions, and three people spoke from the floor, including a Lahaina Strong representative who shared survey results from 834 people. Unresolved items include the final site, how human remains in the ash will be respected, and whether alternatives like pyrolysis or bioremediation will be used. The Mayor said the final site decision will be his, with his advisors.

parts.title: Welcome and meeting format
presented: The meeting was live streamed on the County Facebook page and can be watched later.
Reentry to all 83 zones finished ahead of schedule, so debris removal is the next phase.
No final containment site has been determined yet; several sites are being looked at.
Questions and comments were collected on written cards during the meeting.

next.what: County community forum with Lahaina Strong on any question

parts.title: FEMA overview of cleanup phases
presented: EPA finished Phase 1 removal of household hazardous materials by hand; properties too dangerous to enter will be handled in Phase 2.
The U.S. Coast Guard removed 87 destroyed vessels from Lahaina harbor.
Upcountry debris removal began November 7 and is about halfway done; Lahaina has not started.
For this fire, the program added cars, vessels, foundations, commercial properties and soil sampling and excavation.

parts.title: Army Corps of Engineers debris removal plan
parts.presenter: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Recovery Field Office commander
presented: Recyclable metal and concrete go to Maui facilities first; then crews remove ash and 6 inches of soil within the ash footprint, backfill 3 inches, and scrape up to 12 inches total if tests exceed action levels.
Cultural observers and archaeologists will be on every site and work stops when something sensitive is found.
Trucks will be wrapped in thick plastic (burrito wrapping) and travel along Front Street to the temporary debris storage site at the Olowalu cinder pits.
Debris removal in Lahaina is expected to start mid-January, with the storage site finished in early February and crews expanding over one to two months.

next.what: Debris removal begins in Lahaina and temporary storage site starts receiving material
Final construction of the temporary debris storage site complete

parts.title: Pule
presented: A community member offered a pule and breathing exercise, describing Olowalu as a historic place of refuge.

parts.title: County search for a permanent disposal site
parts.presenter: Director, County Department of Environmental Management
presented: The County scored eight possible sites; Olowalu ranked first, Wahikuli second and Crater Village third, with Central Maui Landfill and Ukumehame tied for fourth.
Scoring covered land acquisition time, distance to Lahaina, homes, schools and drinking water, surface water and environmental impacts; cultural issues were not part of this scoring.
Olowalu sits below the underground injection control line, over brackish rather than drinking water, and has an access road, scale house and water for dust control.
The proposed design has two 80-mil plastic liners in an 8-foot-thick bottom section, a cover liner that sheds water, and leachate, gas and groundwater monitoring.

parts.title: Questions from written cards
presented: Questions were read from cards and answered by County, FEMA and Army Corps officials.

raised.concern: Why not take the debris to Kahoʻolawe?
Why not take the debris off island as first suggested?
When can owners rebuild after debris is removed, and how will they be notified?
When does removal start, how long does it take, and can it be sped up?
Can owners sift through debris for belongings during removal?
Can a right of entry be changed if an engineer finds retaining walls are sound?
What to do when an insurance policy does not cover debris removal
Has bioremediation of the ash been considered?
How is the order of property cleanup decided?
Dust control during offloading and what air monitors test for
How debris will be removed from backyard swimming pools
Respecting human remains in the ash and collecting them separately from other debris
Why heavy equipment was used in Phase 1 without owners being told or giving permission
Is there a protocol for recycling concrete that may leach dioxin?
What Bill 120 does and what a yes or no vote means
Will cesspools in the Wahikuli area be filled and capped?
Who authorized the Olowalu site for temporary and possible permanent use?
How long is temporary storage expected to last?
How long did mainland toxic debris landfills take to build?
Will FEMA help pay for final disposal of the ash and debris?
Who makes the final decision on the permanent site?
How wrapped debris is unloaded at the storage site
Will the land be allowed to rest after debris removal?
Has biochar been considered for the cleanup?

answered.said: Kahoʻolawe was not studied; it would slow removal, but the County is open to looking at it.
Off-island disposal is estimated at $4 billion versus $1 billion on island, and would take about three years and need another storage site at a major harbor.
Building permits get expedited review now or through a new consultant path; when the Army Corps finishes, the County is notified electronically and owners can start building.
Most residential lots take about three to five days; owners get a call 72 hours before work to discuss sensitive items.
Owners cannot enter the site, but protected crew members can sift an area for items on their behalf.
Retaining walls inside the ash footprint are usually unsound and removed; walls outside it usually stay; owners should discuss with crews.
FEMA cannot fund duplicate benefits; the County will collect any debris removal insurance money and leftover rebuild funds, decided case by case.
The County attended a bioremediation presentation and is in talks with developers; cost is not known.
Priority is life and health safety near occupied areas, then environmental risk, then neighborhoods with the most rights of entry submitted.
Crews spray water with every scoop, workers and property edges have monitors, and work stops if alarms trigger; monitors test mainly for heavy metals as directed by the Department of Health.
Pools outside the ash footprint that are structurally sound are not removed.
Observers on site will stop work when remains are found and the needed time will be taken to handle them appropriately.
Phase 1 was done under the state emergency proclamation without rights of entry, by hand only, in about three hours per property.
The answer is not known yet and will be shared at a future meeting.
Bill 120 extends the state right of entry at Olowalu to one year with extension; without it the Army Corps must stop work there on day 91.
Cesspools on properties should not be disturbed; crews need to know their locations to avoid driving over them.
The Board of Land and Natural Resources gave the County a temporary right of entry, and the County licensed the site to the Army Corps.
There is no set number; temporary lasts until a final site is chosen.
Residential fire debris is exempt from federal hazardous waste rules and in California has gone to regular landfills.
FEMA will fund expanding the storage site and transport to the permanent site, including tipping fees.
The final choice will be a collaboration of infrastructure staff, the Mayor's office and the community.
Trucks dump the wrapped load and equipment moves it; it is rewrapped when moved out.

raised.concern: Melted PVC from pipes and wiring may release dioxins, air monitors do not test for dioxin, and residents should not handle PVC on their properties
Explore pyrolysis or turning ash into inert or carbon-negative concrete before choosing a permanent site
Army Corps grading appears to extend into the parcel of the proposed permanent site

Survey of 834 people: 65% strongly agreed with using established landfills or off-island options over new sites, 80% favored separating human remains, 98% want a baseline water study, 97% want alternatives explored

next.what: Lahaina Strong survey stays open and results go to the County

parts.title: Closing remarks
presented: The Mayor questioned the risk of shipping debris across the channel to Kahoʻolawe.
He said the final site decision will be his and his advisors', aiming for the best for the most people.

answered.said: Taking debris to Kahoʻolawe would mean risking transport across the ocean to an island already damaged enough.
The final call on the permanent site will fall on him and his advisors.

next.what: Community meeting in Lahaina, then break from weekly meetings

bills.name: Bill 120
bills.what: Extends the County's right of entry from the state at the Olowalu site to one year with an extension, so the temporary storage site can keep operating.

bills.name: Bill 119
bills.what: Emergency ordinance that let the County manage the Olowalu site under a 90-day temporary right of entry.

not_on_tracker.topic: Choosing a permanent disposal site for Lahaina fire ash and debris
not_on_tracker.why: Residents worry about effects on Olowalu, groundwater and the ocean, and many prefer established landfills or off-island options.

not_on_tracker.topic: Respectful handling of human remains in the ash
not_on_tracker.why: Families who lost loved ones do not want remains mixed with debris and dumped.

not_on_tracker.topic: Dioxins from burned PVC in Lahaina
not_on_tracker.why: A resident fears long-term health harm from touching melted pipes and wiring that monitors may not detect.
